strengths: TAG is a genuinely simple, computationally free (zero extra NFEs) plug-and-play modification that is evaluated consistently across many backbones (SD v1.5/v2.1, SDXL, SD3/flow-matching), samplers (DDIM, DPM++), and guidance stacks (SAG, PAG, SEG, CFG), with consistent FID/IS improvements at matched compute (Tables 1-5).

The geometric framing - decomposing the solver increment into radial (x̂-parallel) and tangential components and reweighting only the tangential part - is intuitive, and the paper correctly identifies that normal amplification distorts the scheduler's radial/SNR calibration (Eq. 16-17, Fig. 4), which is a useful design insight.
The limitation section is honest and analytical: the authors derive the norm blow-up term (η²−1)‖P⊥Δ‖² (Eq. 21) that explains the empirically observed degradation at large η, rather than hiding it.

Implementation is fully specified via pseudo-code (Algorithms 1-2) and PyTorch snippets (Appendix B), making the method easy to reimplement; the proof of Theorem 4.1 is included and its algebra checks out.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is thin and somewhat circular. The 'first-order Taylor gain' G(η) is defined with respect to the model's own score (the true score is replaced by sθ = −εθ/σ in Eq. 25), so the theorem essentially shows that scaling a component of the update that has positive inner product with the score increases the alignment with the score - a near-tautology. Moreover, ∇log p(x|tk+1) is the score of the noisy marginal at tk+1, so the link to 'higher probability on the data manifold' and to 'hallucination reduction' is heuristic at best. Also, Theorem 4.1 states equality holds 'iff η = 1' while the proof says 'or the tangential score component is zero' - an inconsistency.

The central geometric premise - that the direction x/‖x‖ is 'normal' to the data manifold and P⊥Δ is 'tangential' to it - is asserted, not established. The data manifold is not a sphere centered at the origin in latent space; Fig. 2's decoded projections are suggestive but not rigorous evidence that the orthogonal component carries the semantics.

Missing comparison with the most directly related method, TCFG (Kwon et al., 2025), which the paper itself cites as the source of its conditional-generation motivation (tangential CFG with opposite sign). Without this comparison the claimed novelty of 'amplifying vs. damping' the tangential component is not quantified.

Several evaluation setups are confounded: in Table 4, CFG+C-TAG uses 15 steps/30 NFEs vs. 50 steps/100 NFEs for the CFG baseline, so quality differences conflate step count, guidance interval effects, and the TAG modification. The SEG+C-TAG row shows a clear CLIPScore regression (18.17 → 16.94) that is not discussed.

The claim of 'hallucination-resistant' sampling is never measured directly: no hallucination-specific metrics (e.g., attribute binding, TIFA/VQAScore), no human evaluation, and no diversity measures. The evidence for the headline claim rests on FID/IS and cherry-picked qualitative figures. FID standard errors and multi-seed runs are absent.

Absolute FID values (60-125 for unconditional SD vs. ImageNet val) indicate a highly non-standard evaluation regime where SD's LAION training distribution mismatches ImageNet; improvements are real but the setup limits external comparability, and 10K samples (Table 2) is small for stable FID estimation.

The conditional method is inconsistent across its three presentations: Eq. 19-20 (amplify σ⁻¹P(g⊥)εc), Algorithm 2 (normalized projection ⟨εc, g⊥⟩/‖g⊥‖²), and the code in Appendix B (g_aligned = proj(s_c, t_c − t_u), a different quantity entirely). It is unclear which variant produced the reported numbers. The project-page URL is also left blank and no code release is stated, weakening reproducibility.

The effective method - multiply the update's component orthogonal to x̂ by η ≈ 1.1-1.2 - is very simple, and sensitivity is narrow (η > 1.25 degrades); a time-dependent or adaptive η is left to future work, so the practical operating envelope is small and hand-tuned per backbone.

strengths: The proposed TAG is genuinely simple and computationally cheap: it modifies only the post-step update (Algorithm 1) without extra NFEs, and the idea of decomposing the solver increment into radial/tangential parts w.r.t. the current state is intuitive and clearly illustrated (Figures 1-3).

The method is evaluated across several backbones and samplers (SD v1.5/v2.1/SDXL/SD3, DDIM, DPM++, flow matching) and both unconditional and conditional settings, and the reported direction of improvement (FID decrease, IS increase) is consistent, including a hyperparameter ablation on eta (Figure 8) and an honest limitations section that explains the eta-degradation via a norm-perturbation argument (eq. 21).
Implementation code snippets (Appendix B) make the algorithmic variants (TAG and C-TAG) unambiguous and easy to reimplement.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claim is essentially circular and does not support the headline claims. Theorem 4.1 replaces the true score with the model's own noise prediction (eq. 25-26), and since the tangential increment is proportional to the projected noise prediction (eq. 12/32), 'amplifying the tangential component increases the inner product with the score' is trivially true by construction. This first-order dot-product 'gain' says nothing about following the data manifold, avoiding mode interpolation, or reducing hallucination - yet the abstract, contributions, and Theorem 4.1 claim to 'prove' trajectory steering toward the in-distribution manifold. No experiment verifies the log-likelihood gain or manifold-proximity interpretation directly.

Novelty over prior decomposition-based guidance is thin and under-analyzed. TCFG (Kwon et al., 2025) already performs the opposite operation (tangential damping) on the same decomposition, and Sadat et al. (2025) and Hong et al. (2023/2024) already frame guidance as geometry-aware component reweighting. The paper does not compare against TCFG at all, does not explain when amplification rather than damping is appropriate, and the C-TAG variant (eq. 19-20) reads as a minor projection-based modification of CFG.

The empirical protocol has serious credibility problems. FID values are implausibly high and poorly contextualized: SD v1.5 unconditional 'ImageNet' FID of ~77-124 (Tables 1-3) reflects evaluating models never trained on ImageNet against ImageNet statistics, and no standard reference point (e.g., the same models with CFG, or FID on a matched-domain dataset) is provided for the unconditional setting. Several evaluations use only 10K samples (Table 2), where FID bias is large, and no variance/confidence intervals over seeds are reported anywhere. It is also unclear whether eta was tuned on the same data used for reporting, since eta varies per experiment (1.05-1.25) with no held-out tuning protocol.

Key claimed results are under-supported. The headline 'TAG enables 30 NFEs to outperform 100-NFE CFG' (Table 4) compares different step counts and guidance configurations without isolating the effect; the hallucination-reduction claim - the paper's stated motivation - is supported only by cherry-picked qualitative figures (Figures 5-7) and a 2D toy example, with no quantitative hallucination or mode-interpolation metric (e.g., following Aithal et al., 2024, who are cited as motivation).

Presentation and citation sloppiness undermines confidence: equation 1 mislabels the drift/score terms, Theorem 4.1 states G(base) as G(eta=1) while the theorem text also says equality holds 'iff eta = 1' but the proof requires the tangential score to vanish, Figure 6 attributes SD3 to Podell et al. (2024) (which is SDXL), the project-page URL in the introduction is blank, and the reproducibility statement (Section 8) lists only libraries with no code release, making exact reproduction of the FID protocol and eta choices difficult.

The theoretical framing ignores the distributional cost of the modification: eq. 21 shows TAG inflates the state norm, and the paper itself shows performance degrades for moderate eta (>~1.15), meaning the method is a narrow, sensitivity-limited correction whose 'monotonic improvement' guarantee (which is unbounded in eta) directly contradicts the observed behavior - exposing that the first-order analysis does not describe the actual regime of use.

strengths: TAG is a genuinely simple, plug-and-play modification (one projection-based reweighting of the solver increment) with essentially zero computational overhead, and the paper provides clean Algorithm boxes plus reference PyTorch code in Appendix B, which aids implementation.

The empirical evaluation is reasonably broad for a guidance paper: multiple backbones (SD v1.5/v2.1, SDXL, SD3/flow-matching), multiple samplers (DDIM, DPM++), and stacking on top of existing guidance methods (SAG, PAG, SEG, CFG) with consistent FID improvements at matched NFEs, including a compute–quality comparison (Table 3).
The 2D branching-distribution experiment (Figure 3) directly visualizes the claimed mechanism (reduced off-manifold mass) rather than relying only on image metrics.

The limitation section is honest and analytic: Equation 21 explains why large η degrades quality by perturbing the radial calibration, and the authors acknowledge the need for adaptive gains rather than overclaiming.
weaknesses: The central theoretical contribution (Theorem 4.1) is essentially circular and close to trivial. The 'first-order Taylor gain' G(η) is defined as the inner product of the update with the model's own score, evaluated at the same point x_{k+1}; by construction it is linear in η, so monotonicity follows immediately from algebra. It shows only that a larger step along the (approximated) score direction increases a first-order proxy of model density — it does not establish improved sample quality, reduced mode interpolation, or 'hallucination resistance'. The paper repeatedly frames this as 'proving that amplifying the tangential steers trajectories toward the in-distribution manifold', which the theorem does not support.

The claimed link to hallucination is not measured. No direct hallucination metric (e.g., attribute-binding or mode-interpolation benchmarks in the style of Aithal et al., 2024, who motivate the paper) is evaluated; the 'hallucination-resistant' claim rests on FID/IS and cherry-picked qualitative figures.

Novelty relative to closely related work is under-argued. The normal/tangential decomposition of guidance updates is well established (TCFG, Kwon et al. 2025; Sadat et al., 2025 are cited but not empirically compared); TAG is essentially the amplification counterpart of TCFG's tangential damping. A head-to-head comparison or a sharper differentiation of the mechanism is missing.

Hyperparameter sensitivity is a core weakness: gains exist only in a very narrow range (η ≈ 1.05–1.25) and degrade by η = 1.25–1.3 (Table 1, Figure 8), yet only 3–4 values of η are ever reported, η is applied uniformly across all timesteps, and no tuning protocol or guidance is given for practitioners.

Internal inconsistencies undermine confidence in the method description: Equation 20 (using σ_k^{-1}P(g⊥)ε_c) does not match Algorithm 2 (normalized projection ⟨ε_c,g⊥⟩/||g⊥||²), and the appendix code (Algorithm 4, projecting s_c onto t_c − t_u and modifying g differently) matches neither; Table 2/6 also mis-cite SD3 as Podell et al. (2024), and footnote 1's project page URL is empty.

The evaluation protocol is nonstandard and hard to contextualize: unconditional SD v1.5 evaluated against the ImageNet val set yields very high FIDs (60–125), and Table 4 reports CLIPScore where the claimed improvement fails for SEG+C-TAG (18.17 → 16.94) despite the text asserting consistent gains.

Reproducibility is weak: no code release is stated (only a library-list 'reproducibility statement'), fixed seeds are mentioned but per-experiment configurations (per-timestep η, exact scheduler coefficients for DPM++, CFG combination details) are incomplete.
